notes: Fixed slots 2,3,4,6,8,9,12,18,19,21,22,23 left untouched. Slot 13 = Revolutionary Command Council as the state apex (al-Bakr chair, Saddam vice-chair since Nov 1969), kept distinct from the Ba'ath Party in 21. Slot 7 = Saddam's party security apparatus Jihaz Hanin with Nadhim Kazzar's General Security. Slot 0 = pro-Western exiles around al-Nayif and al-Rawi (Iran-backed plotting on the eve of the Jan 1970 coup attempt). Slot 5 = ICP Central Command (Aziz al-Hajj split). Slot 11 = Hizb ut-Tahrir's Iraqi branch. Slot 20 = Qasimite populists. No MD IRQ sprite depicts these 1970 organizations, so all icons are null.

0.name: Rijal al-Nayif
0.text:
Al-Nayif's Men are the exiled officers, politicians and tribal sheikhs gathered around Abd al-Razzaq al-Nayif, the former deputy chief of military intelligence who served as prime minister for thirteen days after the coup of July 1968 until the Ba'athists expelled him. Their allies include the retired general Abd al-Ghani al-Rawi, who plots from Iran with the Shah's money and protection.

They stand for a conservative, pro-Western military government: an end to Ba'athist terror, reconciliation with Iran and the Gulf monarchies, renewed ties with Britain and the United States, and the suppression of communism. Their base lies among purged officers, dispossessed landlords and southern tribes. Their leverage is foreign backing and the hope that one coup can undo another.

1.name: Al-Kanisa al-Kaldaniyya al-Kathulikiyya
1.text:
The Chaldean Catholic Church is the largest Christian community in Iraq, an Eastern church in full communion with Rome, led from Baghdad by Patriarch Paul II Cheikho of Babylon. Its faithful live in Baghdad, Mosul and Basra and in the villages of the Nineveh plain and the northern mountains, where many are caught between the Kurdish war and the army.

The church stands for a cautious Christian conservatism: protection of its schools, property and community life, good relations with whichever government rules, and close ties to the Vatican and the Catholic West. It opposes communism and fears Arab and Kurdish nationalism alike. Its leverage lies in an educated urban middle class, foreign connections and its role as mediator between Christians and the state.

5.name: Al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Iraqi – al-Qiyada al-Markaziyya
5.text:
The Iraqi Communist Party – Central Command broke away from the official party in September 1967, accusing its leaders of passivity, and turned to armed struggle. In 1968 its guerrillas under Khalid Ahmad Zaki opened a front in the southern marshes until he was killed, and in 1969 its leader Aziz al-Hajj was captured and recanted on television.

Its surviving cells of students, intellectuals and marsh peasants still preach revolutionary war on the Guevarist and Maoist model, denounce the official communists' accommodation with the Ba'ath and scorn Soviet-style peaceful coexistence. Hunted by the security services and shaken by betrayal, it is small, but the legend of the marsh guerrilla still draws young radicals to its ranks.

7.name: Jihaz Hanin
7.text:
Jihaz Hanin, the ‘Instrument of Yearning’, is the secret security apparatus Saddam Hussein built inside the Ba'ath Party in the 1960s, now fused with the state since he became vice-chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council in November 1969. Its men dominate the Directorate of General Security under Nadhim Kazzar and the interrogation cells of the Palace of the End.

Its creed is Ba'athist power without limits: the eradication of plotters, communists, Islamists and ‘spies’, the subordination of the army to the party and personal loyalty to Saddam above all. It favours Soviet arms and Arab socialism but serves no foreign master. Its leverage is fear, files and the readiness to kill, which make it the true engine of the regime.

10.name: Ulama' al-A'zamiyya
10.text:
The Ulama of al-A'zamiyya are the Sunni scholars and preachers clustered around the Abu Hanifa Mosque in Baghdad's al-A'zamiyya quarter, together with the Hanafi establishment of mosques, colleges and endowments supervised by the Ministry of Awqaf. Licensed and salaried by the state, they are the official voice of Sunni Islam in the capital.

They preach a quietist, conservative Islam: obedience to rulers who allow prayer, opposition to atheism and communism, respect for sharia in family law and good relations with Saudi Arabia and the Gulf monarchies. They avoid open challenge to the Ba'ath while resenting its secularism. Their leverage is the pulpit and the Friday sermon, heard across Sunni Baghdad.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir al-Islami
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, who now directs it from Beirut, has had an Iraqi branch since the 1950s, recruiting students, teachers and junior officers in Baghdad, Mosul and Ramadi. Banned and hunted, it lost an outspoken ally when the preacher Abd al-Aziz al-Badri, once close to the party, died in Ba'athist custody in 1969.

Its aim is the restoration of the caliphate across the Muslim world, to be won by gaining the support of the army and seizing power, after which existing states, parties and borders would be swept away. It rejects nationalism, Ba'athism, communism and Western democracy alike. Its leverage is disciplined secrecy and its appeal to officers, the one constituency that makes coups.

13.name: Majlis Qiyadat al-Thawra
13.text:
The Revolutionary Command Council is the supreme organ of state created by the coup of 17 July 1968, ruling by decree under its chairman, President Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr. Since November 1969 Saddam Hussein has been its vice-chairman, and its members include the officer-ministers Hardan al-Tikriti and Salih Mahdi Ammash.

It embodies a non-aligned, state-centred authoritarianism: central planning, land reform, nationalisation and the drive to wrest control of oil from the Iraq Petroleum Company. It balances between Moscow and the West and tolerates no rival. Its leverage is total legal authority, though behind its façade the civilian and military wings of the Ba'ath compete for control.

14.name: Shuyukh al-Furat
14.text:
The Sheikhs of the Euphrates are the leaders of the great tribes of the middle and lower Euphrates: the Fatla, Bani Hasan and Khaza'il, whose forebears rose against the British in 1920, and the clans of the old Muntafiq confederation. The agrarian reform of 1958 stripped many of their estates, but they still command the loyalty of tribesmen and hold court in their madifs.

They stand for tribal custom, landed property, religious tradition and local autonomy against both Ba'athist centralism and communist land seizures. They belong to neither bloc and bargain with whoever rules in Baghdad. Their leverage lies in armed kinsmen, rural patronage and the state's continuing need for intermediaries in the countryside.

15.name: Ghurfat Tijarat Baghdad
15.text:
The Baghdad Chamber of Commerce represents the importers, wholesalers, contractors and industrialists of the capital. Once led by Jewish, Shia and Sunni merchant houses, it was shaken by the nationalisation of banks, insurance and large industry in July 1964 and by the destruction of the Jewish community, whose last members live in fear after the public hangings of January 1969.

It speaks for property, contracts and private enterprise: compensation for nationalisations, import licences, access to foreign credit and a return of business confidence. It avoids open politics, preferring quiet bargains with ministers. Its leverage is economic, for the regime still needs merchants to feed Baghdad, import machinery and keep the markets supplied.

16.name: Tujjar al-Shorja
16.text:
The Shorja Traders are the shopkeepers, wholesalers, money changers and smugglers of Baghdad's great Shorja market and the bazaars of Basra, Mosul and Najaf. Mostly self-made, many from Shia and Faili Kurdish families, they operate in the gaps between state monopolies, price controls and the border trade with Iran, Kuwait and Syria.

They want free trade, low taxes, no price controls and a state that leaves the bazaar alone. Indifferent to grand ideologies and to both superpowers, they judge every government by its effect on business. Their leverage is that Baghdad's daily life runs through their shops, and they can starve or flood the market at will.

17.name: Ahl al-Ahwar
17.text:
The People of the Marshes are the Ma'dan, the buffalo herders, fishermen and reed weavers of the great wetlands where the Tigris and Euphrates meet, together with the sheikhs and teachers who speak for them. Their world of reed houses and canoes has endured for millennia, but drainage plans and the hunt for guerrillas in the reed beds now press upon it.

They seek protection for the marshes as a living landscape: an end to drainage and diversion schemes, respect for fishing and grazing rights, and schools and clinics that do not require destroying the reed beds. They distrust Baghdad's planners. Their leverage is that the marshes are impenetrable to armies and home to several hundred thousand people.

20.name: Al-Qasimiyyun
20.text:
The Qasimites are the loyalists of Abd al-Karim Qasim, the ‘sole leader’ who overthrew the monarchy in 1958 and was shot by the Ba'athists in February 1963. His memory lives on among the poor of al-Thawra, the township he built for migrants from the south, among old soldiers and in villages that received land under his reform.

Their creed is Iraq-first patriotism: Iraq for the Iraqis rather than for pan-Arab dreams, social justice, land reform and a strong leader standing above the parties. They hate the Ba'ath for Qasim's death and distrust the Nasserists. Lacking any organisation, their leverage is popular emotion and numbers that any demagogue invoking Qasim's name could still mobilise.
